description: We’re a student team from Surabaya, Indonesia, interested in electrical and computer engineering. For NASA Space Apps’ Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, we built Lunar Window Planner, a web tool that uses NASA data to compare potential sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility at lunar south pole landing sites. Our goal is to make a practical engineering decision easy to explore: where and when should a lander touch down if it needs sunlight for power and to report back to Earth.
summary:
Lunar Window is an interactive planner for comparing landing sites and touchdown times near the lunar south pole. It combines NASA elevation and ephemeris data to show when terrain hides Earth or the Sun. In a 24-hour example, adding terrain changes the site with the shortest modeled Earth blackout from Malapert Massif to de Gerlache Rim 2. Moving the de Gerlache touchdown six hours later reduces its wait for an Earth sightline from 7.66 to 1.66 hours, meeting a two-hour geometric check-in deadline. Users can explore the result on a shared timeline and skyline view, compare potential sunlight and download the modeled intervals.

Project files and supporting folders (Google Drive): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1NfJmiWU7LitZFKUrkLqIlHxxYbBT6A-F
details:
Lunar Window helps planners compare when a lander may first see Earth, how long a continuous Earth blackout could last, and when sunlight could reach a solar observer. The prototype covers five south-pole sites and 36 days starting 14 November 2026 UTC. It supports 1-hour to 30-day windows, 2 m and 5 m antenna cases, and CSV export.

Method. Ten-minute NASA JPL Horizons samples are projected into a local observer frame. LRO LOLA elevation grids provide a skyline at each bearing. The model subtracts the skyline angle from the Sun or Earth center elevation, interpolates crossings between samples, and reports uncertain intervals where coverage prevents a clear result. The flat reference uses a zero-degree skyline.

Results. For the 24 hours starting 17 November 2026 at 00:00 UTC, the longest Earth blackout at 2 m is 0.00 h at Malapert Massif and 1.12 h at de Gerlache Rim 2 with the flat reference. With LOLA terrain it is 20.48 h and 7.66 h, respectively. At 5 m with terrain it is 10.89 h and 7.60 h. For touchdown at 06:00 UTC at 2 m with terrain, de Gerlache reaches a first Earth sightline after 1.66 h versus 14.48 h for Malapert. In the original 00:00 UTC terrain scenario, both sites have zero hours of modeled Sun-center visibility, while Shackleton Rim has 24 hours of modeled Sun-center visibility and zero hours of Earth-center visibility.

Validation and limits. Six archived Horizons queries provide 10,374 paired comparisons. The maximum projection differences are 0.000002° in bearing and 0.000001° in elevation, with terrain held fixed. Running the demo coordinates through the coarser custom pipeline shifts the 2 m outage estimates to 11.53 h at Malapert and 8.23 h at de Gerlache. These are geometric screening estimates. A radio link analysis and an energy budget account separately for antenna pointing, link margin, station schedules, panel orientation, and irradiance.

Implementation and reproducibility. JavaScript, HTML, CSS and a Web Worker run the planner. Python and NumPy prepare and validate the data. The repository contains the source, terrain grids, archived Horizons responses, reproducibility scripts, tests, CSV and credits: https://github.com/fowlu/lunar-window-planner

AI-use disclosure. ChatGPT helped develop and implement the website’s visuals, especially the user interface. Team members directed, reviewed, and revised the design and implementation. The project concept and engineering questions originated with the team. The source package includes optional local Ollama commentary. The planner computes the results and rankings from the NASA data.
